paragraphs.heading: The farthest planet
paragraphs.text: Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun and the farthest one known. It ranks fourth in diameter and third in mass, at 17 times the mass of Earth, and it is the densest of the giant planets. Next to its neighbour Uranus it is a little smaller but heavier and denser. Made mostly of gases and liquids, it has no clear solid surface. It takes 164.8 years to go once around the Sun, at a distance of 4.5 billion kilometres.

paragraphs.heading: An ice giant
paragraphs.text: Like Jupiter and Saturn, Neptune has an atmosphere made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with traces of hydrocarbons and perhaps nitrogen. But it holds a larger share of ices such as water, ammonia and methane. Its interior, like that of Uranus, is mainly ices and rock, so the two are usually called ice giants to set them apart. Rayleigh scattering and traces of methane high in the atmosphere give Neptune a faint blue look.

paragraphs.heading: Found by mathematics
paragraphs.text: Neptune cannot be seen with the naked eye, and it is the only planet that was not first found by looking. Instead, Uranus kept straying from where its orbit was expected to be, and Alexis Bouvard suggested that an unknown planet was tugging on it by gravity. After Bouvard died, John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier each worked out, separately, where that planet should be. On 23 September 1846, Johann Gottfried Galle spotted it through a telescope within a degree of Le Verrier's predicted spot. Its largest moon, Triton, was found soon after.

paragraphs.heading: Seen but not recognised
paragraphs.text: Others saw Neptune earlier without knowing it. Galileo's drawings from December 1612 and January 1613 mark points that match where Neptune was on those dates, but he seems to have taken it for a fixed star near Jupiter, so he does not get the credit. After Le Verrier's estimate appeared in June 1846, James Challis searched in vain through August and September. He had in fact recorded Neptune twice in August 1845, a year before Galle, but outdated star maps and poor technique kept him from realising it until later.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to study
paragraphs.text: Because it is so distant, Neptune looks small and dim from Earth, which makes it hard to study with ground-based telescopes. Detailed views came only with the Hubble Space Telescope and large ground telescopes using adaptive optics. Voyager 2, which passed it on 25 August 1989, is still the only spacecraft to have visited. Neptune also has a faint, broken ring system, called arcs, found in 1984 and confirmed by Voyager 2.

paragraphs.heading: Wild weather
paragraphs.text: Unlike Uranus, whose strongly seasonal atmosphere can look blank for long stretches, Neptune shows active weather that stays visible. During the Voyager 2 flyby, a Great Dark Spot sat in the southern hemisphere, comparable to Jupiter's Great Red Spot, and in 2018 a newer main dark spot and a smaller one were studied. Behind this weather are the fastest steady winds found on any planet, up to 2,100 km/h. Being so far from the Sun, the top of its atmosphere ranks among the coldest spots in the Solar System, with cloud tops near 55 K (−218 °C), while its centre is about 5,400 K.
